/fr/articles/apprendre-le-coran-a-son-en.title: Teaching your child the Quran: why and how | Rewayah
/fr/articles/apprendre-le-coran-a-son-en.description: Why pass the Quran on to your child, what tradition built around it for centuries, and how to go about it, close to home or at a distance.
/fr/articles/apprendre-le-coran-a-son-en.h1: Teaching your child the Quran: why it matters so much, and how to go about it
/fr/articles/apprendre-le-coran-a-son-en.intro: Passing the Quran on to your child means giving them a language to pray in, a text that will stay with them all their life, and a memory that links them to those who came before. Far from Quran schools, this does not happen by itself any more: it has to be decided. Here is why it matters so much, what Muslim tradition built around it for centuries, and how to put it in place today.

sections.title: The first word revealed: the command to read
paragraphs: The revelation of the Quran begins with a command to read. The first verses sent down to the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) open Surah Al-Alaq (Quran 96:1-5): they tell him to read in the name of his Lord who created, who created man from a clinging substance, and they recall that his Lord, the Most Generous, taught by the pen and taught man what he did not know.

The hadith of Aisha, reported by al-Bukhari at the very start of his collection (no. 3, and no. 4953 for the full passage), relates that the revelation began with these verses; another account, also reported by al-Bukhari, mentions the opening of Surah Al-Muddaththir (no. 4922). The message therefore opens with reading, knowledge and the pen. Teaching a child to read the Quran means bringing them into this story through its very first door.

sections.title: A responsibility entrusted to parents
paragraphs: The Quran speaks directly to believers about their families: in Surah At-Tahrim (Quran 66:6), it calls on those who believe to protect themselves and their families from a Fire whose fuel is people and stones.

The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) summed up this responsibility in a simple image: each of you is a shepherd, and each of you is responsible for his flock (reported by al-Bukhari, no. 893, and Muslim, no. 1829 a). A parent does not have to teach everything themselves. But it is up to them to make sure their child learns, and to choose with whom and at what pace.

This responsibility is also an opportunity. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said that the best among you is the one who learns the Quran and teaches it (reported by al-Bukhari, no. 5027). A parent who has their child learn the Quran, and who sometimes learns it alongside them, is included in these words.

sections.title: What tradition built around the Quran
paragraphs: For centuries, in Muslim cities, a child’s education began with the Quran. They learned it at the kuttab, a modest elementary school where pupils mainly memorised the Quran, with a teacher.

In the 14th century, the historian Ibn Khaldun already wrote about this in his Muqaddimah. He counts teaching the Quran to children among the distinctive marks of Muslim civilisation, a custom believers adopted and followed in all their great cities, because verses and traditions learned early firmly root the articles of faith in a child’s heart. For him, the Quran is therefore the basis of teaching and the foundation of all the knowledge acquired later. (Les Prolégomènes, French translation by William Mac Guckin de Slane, part three, 1868, p. 285; where that translation says “Muslim civilisation”, the Arabic literally says “religion”.)

The Quran was not passed on through books alone. Scholars of recitation point this out: it was passed on by word of mouth, from teacher to student, through unbroken chains that go back to the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him). Every child who learns with a teacher takes their place in that chain.

sections.title: Why it is urgent today
paragraphs: Many families now live in the West, and wherever Muslims are a minority, far from these schools. Children grow up between two worlds: home, and a society where the language of the Quran is almost never heard. Without someone passing it on, prayer becomes a string of sounds no one can read any more, and the Quran a book people respect without being able to open it.

This uprooting, both religious and cultural, does not happen in a day. It moves forward quietly, from one generation to the next, when no one takes over. On the other hand, a child who can read the Quran, who knows some surahs by heart and who knows where what they recite comes from, keeps a firm footing. They know where they belong, even when everything around them speaks another language.
That is why the way you teach matters as much as the decision to teach.

sections.title: Close to home or at a distance: how to choose
paragraphs: If good in-person Quran teaching exists near you, start there. Nothing replaces a classroom, a mosque, a teacher your child meets and your family knows. Distance learning is a valuable solution for families for whom this is not possible; it should not be a default choice.

Either way, look at what the teaching actually organises rather than what it promises: an appointed teacher, who knows your child’s mistakes and follows their progress; a small, stable class, where everyone is heard; a fixed schedule that comes back every week, because regular attendance is built on routine; a step-by-step programme, with dates; visible follow-up, and written terms.

Ask your questions in writing before you commit. Who will the teacher be, and will they stay the same? What happens if they are absent? How will you be told about progress? Can you sit in on a session? Be wary, on the other hand, of a promise of quick results, of pressure to pay straight away, or of a title put forward without anyone knowing what training it belongs to.

sections.title: What home can do, every day
paragraphs: The teacher teaches; home makes it last. A few minutes a day, at a fixed time, are worth more than a long preparation the night before class. Listen to your child recite; correct a mistake gently, without turning it into a second session, and name their progress.

And, when you can, let them hear you read. A child also learns from what they see others do: a parent who opens the Quran at home teaches, without a word, that this Book has its place in everyday life.

/fr/articles/enfant-fatigue-assiduite.title: Tired child: regular Quran study without conflict | Rewayah
/fr/articles/enfant-fatigue-assiduite.description: Tiredness, boredom or refusal: what your child is going through, what Muslim scholars already said about it, and how to help them keep going, gently.
/fr/articles/enfant-fatigue-assiduite.h1: My child is tired: how to keep up regular Quran study without conflict
/fr/articles/enfant-fatigue-assiduite.intro: Three sessions a week, after school, is demanding. One day your child sighs as they open their book, drags their feet before the session or says they can’t take any more, and you wonder whether to insist or let go. Muslim tradition has known this tiredness for a long time, and it has precise things to say about it. Here is how to understand it, and how to help your child keep going, firmly and gently.

sections.title: A long road, which is sometimes tiring
paragraphs: Learning the Quran does not take a few weeks. A child first learns the letters, then reading with vowel marks, then reading in the Quran and the first surahs, and each step takes months of regular effort. On such a long road, tiredness is not an accident: it is part of the journey, for children as for adults. It does not mean your child is not made for learning; it often means that something in their rhythm needs adjusting.

The Quran sets a measure every parent can keep in mind: in Surah Al-Baqarah (Quran 2:286), it states that Allah does not burden any soul beyond what it can bear. This verse speaks of what Allah asks of His servants; it also teaches anyone who raises a child a sense of measure. The load given to a child must fit their size: demanding enough for them to progress, never so heavy that it crushes them.

And Surah Ash-Sharh repeats the same promise twice in a row (Quran 94:5-6): with hardship comes ease. The difficulty of a child stumbling over a letter is never alone. Often, the parent’s role is to help them see the ease that comes with it: what they already know, how far they have come, and the next step, which is not so high.

sections.title: Tiredness, boredom or refusal: three different situations
paragraphs: Before acting, you need to know what you are dealing with. Tiredness shows at the end of the day: attention drops, eyes sting, but your child still wants to go. It calls for simple answers: sleep, meals, the time of day.

Boredom is something else. Your child already knows the material, or on the contrary can no longer keep up. Then you need to talk to the teacher, to check that the level is right. Refusal, finally, shows up before your child has even tried. It often hides a specific cause: fear of making mistakes in front of others, tension at home around the session. Start by listening.
If the tiredness lasts, goes beyond learning or comes with anxiety, talk to a health professional. No method replaces their advice.

sections.title: What scholars already said about the tired child
paragraphs: Long before modern studies, Muslim scholars looked closely at the tiredness of a child who is learning. In the 11th century, Imam al-Ghazali devoted a passage of his Revival of the Religious Sciences (Ihya’ ‘ulum ad-din) to the education of children. He writes that after leaving school (the kuttab), a child should be allowed to play a good game that rests them from the fatigue of school, without tiring themselves out playing. For him, keeping a child from playing and forcing them to study without a break deadens their heart, ruins their intelligence and makes their life bitter, to the point that they look for a way to escape study altogether. (Ihya’ ‘ulum ad-din, volume 3, p. 73, Dar al-Ma’rifa edition.)

Al-Ghazali was not a lax educator: the same chapter calls for discipline. But he knew that an exhausted child no longer learns, and that too much pressure eventually makes them run away from what we wanted to pass on. For him, play is not a reward handed out when everything is done; it is the rest that makes it possible to come back the next day.

Three centuries later, Ibn Khaldun devoted a chapter of his Muqaddimah to this question. Its title, in de Slane’s French translation, is blunt: too much severity in teaching harms students. He explains that being too harsh with children, especially when they are still very young, is very harmful to them, because it gives their mind a bad disposition, inclines them to laziness and leads them to lie. And he concludes that a tutor should not be too severe with his students, nor a father with his children. (Les Prolégomènes, French translation by William Mac Guckin de Slane, part three, 1868, pp. 290-291.)
Ibn Khaldun does not ask us to give up all expectations; he warns against excess. That is the balance every parent is looking for: keeping the appointment, without turning the session into an ordeal.

citations_arabes.legende: Arabic text: al-Ghazali, Ihya’ ‘ulum ad-din, volume 3, p. 73 (Dar al-Ma’rifa edition)

sections.title: The one who recites with difficulty has two rewards
paragraphs: Tradition offers precious comfort here. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said that the one who recites the Quran skilfully will be with the noble and righteous scribe angels, and that the one who recites it stumbling, finding it hard, will have two rewards (reported by Muslim, no. 798 a; in similar terms by al-Bukhari, no. 4937).

These words change how we see things. The effort of a child who stumbles over the letters is not a delay: it is rewarded. Tell your child so, in simple words. And tell yourself too: your patience is part of this work.
The Quran itself reassures, and this verse comes back four times in Surah Al-Qamar (Quran 54:17): Allah has made the Quran easy to reflect on, and asks whether there is anyone who will take heed.

sections.title: Gentleness, a way of teaching
paragraphs: The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) told Aisha that Allah is Gentle and loves gentleness in all things (reported by al-Bukhari, no. 6927). He also said that gentleness is never in anything without making it beautiful, and is never taken out of anything without making it ugly (reported by Muslim, no. 2594).

He lived this gentleness with those around him, and with children. Anas ibn Malik relates that he served the Prophet for ten years, and that he never once said to him so much as “uff”, nor asked him why he had done something or why he had not done it (reported by al-Bukhari, no. 6038, and Muslim, no. 2309). And the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said that he would begin the prayer intending to make it long, then hear a child crying and shorten it, because he disliked causing hardship to the child’s mother (reported by al-Bukhari, no. 707, and Muslim, no. 470). If the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) shortened the prayer so as not to burden a mother, a parent can certainly, one evening, shorten an exhausted child’s preparation, without giving up the session.

He even made tenderness towards the young a sign of belonging: he said that whoever does not show mercy to our young and does not honour our elders is not one of us (reported by at-Tirmidhi, no. 1920, and Abu Dawud, no. 4943).
Firmness and gentleness are therefore not opposites. You keep the appointment of the session; you soften the way you get there.

citations_arabes.legende: Arabic text: Jami’ at-Tirmidhi, no. 1920

sections.title: Regularity matters more than length
paragraphs: The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said that the deeds most loved by Allah are those done consistently, even if they are few (reported by al-Bukhari, no. 6464, and Muslim, no. 783 b). These words apply to learning the Quran as to every deed: a little, but every day.

Research on learning points in the same direction. Studies that compare methods generally show that spreading work out over time helps people remember better than cramming it into one go; they also rank testing yourself on what you have just learned among the most useful methods. Ask your child to recite to you, without looking, what they already know.

Sleep matters as much as method. Since 2016, a learned society of sleep medicine has recommended 9 to 12 hours of sleep per 24 hours between the ages of 6 and 12, and 8 to 10 hours between 13 and 18; it links regularly shorter sleep to difficulties with attention, behaviour and learning. Before talking about motivation, look at bedtime.

citations_arabes.texte: أَحَبُّ الأَعْمَالِ إِلَى اللَّهِ تَعَالَى أَدْوَمُهَا وَإِنْ قَلَّ
citations_arabes.legende: Arabic text: Sahih Muslim, no. 783 b

sections.title: What you can do at home
paragraphs: Set up a routine: the same time, the same place, the same materials. A fixed framework spares your child a daily negotiation. The session is not up for discussion; the preparation is what you adjust.

Get what is needed ready the day before, and check the connection ahead of time, so the session starts calmly. Keep preparation short: the work to prepare before the next class, nothing more. And, as al-Ghazali advised, give your child a real moment of play, which rests them without wearing them out.

You can also correct them, wisely. Ask them to recite what they know to you; if they make a mistake, correct it gently, one at a time, without stopping them at every word, and finish with encouragement. Choose the moment and keep it short: your child should not feel that class follows them everywhere, or that the Quran is a chore. If the same mistake keeps coming back, tell their teacher, who will work on it in class. Finally, name their small victories: a surah finished, a step completed, a reading without hesitation.

Finally, there is what home does in silence: the parents’ prayer. The Quran relates the prayer of Ibrahim (Quran 14:40), who asks his Lord to make him and some of his descendants steadfast in prayer, and to accept his supplication. And it describes the servants of the Most Merciful (Quran 25:74) as those who ask their Lord to grant them, in their spouses and children, the comfort of their eyes, and to make them an example for the God-fearing. Praying for our children also reminds us that their success does not depend on our efforts alone.

sections.title: What is best avoided
paragraphs: Do not compare your child with their brothers and sisters, or with other students. Never use the Quran as a punishment, and do not threaten to take it away: your child must not associate the Book with fear. Avoid correcting their mistakes in front of the class or the teacher, and avoid shouting just before the session.

The Prophet’s instruction (peace and blessings be upon him) sums up this attitude: make things easy and do not make them hard, give good news and do not drive people away (reported by al-Bukhari, no. 69).

citations_arabes.texte: يَسِّرُوا وَلاَ تُعَسِّرُوا، وَبَشِّرُوا وَلاَ تُنَفِّرُوا
citations_arabes.legende: Arabic text: Sahih al-Bukhari, no. 69

sections.title: When to talk to the teacher
paragraphs: Talk to them as soon as the tiredness or refusal lasts more than a few weeks, or as soon as your child says they are afraid of the session. Describe what you observe, with facts, and ask for a review. At Rewayah, you can write to support, who will answer you in writing.

/fr/articles/apprendre-le-coran-seul-san.description: Why the Quran has been passed from teacher to student since the Prophet, what a student on their own cannot hear, and how to get corrected, even from afar.
/fr/articles/apprendre-le-coran-seul-san.h1: Learning the Quran alone, without a teacher: the risks, and how to avoid them
/fr/articles/apprendre-le-coran-seul-san.intro: Apps, videos, recorded courses: it has never been so easy to start reading the Quran on your own. That is good news, on one condition: not mistaking the tools for a teacher. Here is why the Quran has always been passed on by word of mouth, what a student on their own cannot hear, and how to get corrected, even from afar.

sections.title: The Quran was passed on by word of mouth
paragraphs: The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) himself received the Quran by listening. In Surah Al-Qiyamah (Quran 75:16-18), Allah tells him not to move his tongue to hasten its recitation: gathering it in his heart and its recitation are Allah’s charge, and when Allah recites it, he is to follow its recitation.

Every Ramadan, he studied it with the angel Jibril, as Ibn Abbas reports: Jibril would meet him every night of Ramadan and study the Quran with him (reported by al-Bukhari, no. 6). So the one who received the Quran also had someone to study it with.

The Companions followed this model. Abdullah ibn Mas’ud said, swearing by Allah, that he had learned some seventy surahs directly from the mouth of the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) (reported by al-Bukhari, no. 5000). And the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) directed those who wanted to learn towards specific teachers; Abdullah ibn Amr reports that he told people to take the Quran from four: Abdullah ibn Mas’ud, Salim, Mu’adh and Ubayy ibn Ka’b (reported by al-Bukhari, no. 4999).

sections.title: What a teacher does that a book does not
paragraphs: The Quran describes the Prophet’s mission (peace and blessings be upon him) in Surah Al-Jumu’ah (Quran 62:2): Allah sent to a people without a Book a Messenger from among them, who recites His verses to them, purifies them and teaches them the Book and wisdom. Reciting, purifying, teaching: passing on the Quran is not just a text you receive, it is a person who recites in front of you, listens to you and corrects you.

The Quran also calls for a measured recitation: in Surah Al-Muzzammil (Quran 73:4), it commands reciting the Quran slowly and clearly. This way of reciting is not learned by reading rules; it is heard, imitated and corrected.
And when we do not know, the Quran shows the way: in Surah An-Nahl (Quran 16:43), it tells us to ask the people of remembrance if we do not know.

sections.title: What a student on their own cannot hear
paragraphs: The first difficulty is not reading, but pronouncing well. Arabic distinguishes sounds that French and English do not tell apart. Qāf and kāf are not pronounced in the same place in the mouth: qalb, with a qāf, means “heart”; kalb, with a kāf, means “dog”. The same gap separates ḥā’ from hā’, ‘ayn from hamza, ṣād from sīn. A single letter in the wrong place can change the meaning of a word.

The great master of recitation Ibn al-Jazari, who died in 1429, distinguishes two kinds of mistakes. The obvious mistake (al-laḥn al-jaliyy) affects the words, and it can change their meaning: reading an‘amtu or an‘amti instead of an‘amta in Al-Fatiha makes the verse say that the speaker has bestowed favour, instead of You, Allah, having bestowed it. The hidden mistake (al-laḥn al-khafiyy) does not change the meaning, but it spoils the recitation: an r rolled too much, a nasal n, a thickened l. And he points out that only an accomplished and rigorous reciter, who received the recitation from the mouths of teachers, recognises this hidden mistake (at-Tamhid fi ‘ilm at-tajwid, pp. 21-22).

Finally, there is habit. A mistake repeated a hundred times is no longer heard: it becomes the way you read. The older it is, the longer it takes to correct. That is true of any language; it is even more true of a text you recite every day in prayer.

sections.title: Apps, videos, Latin letters: good tools, not teachers
paragraphs: Listening to recognised reciters, revising with an app, following an explanation on video: all of this helps, and many people found their first spark there. But a tool does not know your mistakes. It does not ask you to start again, it does not tell you that you are mixing up two letters, and it does not adapt to your voice.

Reading in Latin letters raises a particular problem: several Arabic letters have no equivalent in French or English, and transliteration only writes them approximately. Reading the Quran in Latin letters often locks in these approximations. It is better to learn the Arabic letters, even slowly.

sections.title: Reading alone is not forbidden; learning without being heard is risky
paragraphs: This is not about discouraging anyone who reads on their own. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) promised a double reward to the one who recites with difficulty: he said that the one who recites the Quran skilfully will be with the noble and righteous scribe angels, and that the one who recites it stumbling, finding it hard, will have two rewards (reported by Muslim, no. 798 a; in similar terms by al-Bukhari, no. 4937). Personal reading, revision, listening: all of this is good.
What is risky is learning without ever being heard by someone who knows. The answer is not to stop everything, but to have your recitation heard regularly by a teacher.

citations_arabes.texte: الْمَاهِرُ بِالْقُرْآنِ مَعَ السَّفَرَةِ الْكِرَامِ الْبَرَرَةِ وَالَّذِي يَقْرَأُ الْقُرْآنَ وَيَتَتَعْتَعُ فِيهِ وَهُوَ عَلَيْهِ شَاقٌّ لَهُ أَجْرَانِ

sections.title: How to get corrected, even from afar
paragraphs: First look for a teacher near you: a mosque, an association, a Quran school. If that is not possible, distance teaching can play this role, provided it makes you recite and corrects you.

Recite at a fixed time, to the same person, and start with what you think you already know: that is where habits hide. Write down the corrections, go back over them, and ask to be heard again. It is slow, and that is how you progress.
At Rewayah Academy, every student recites to the same teacher, three times a week. If our way does not suit you, others exist, run by other people.

/fr/articles/apprendre-le-coran-en-group.h1: Learning the Quran in a group: why an ambitious class takes you further
/fr/articles/apprendre-le-coran-en-group.intro: The Quran has never been so accessible: online, on your phone, in audio, with its explanations and all the sciences around it. Yet many people start and few keep going. The problem is no longer finding something to read. It is starting, and continuing. That is where a guided group changes everything.

sections.title: Everything is available, and yet we don’t move forward
paragraphs: Today the Quran can be opened in a few seconds on a screen, with many recitations and translations. Classes, talks and explanations abound. This abundance is a blessing; it has not made people more learned for all that. Having access to knowledge does not mean acquiring it.

What is most often missing is not content, but consistency. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said that the deeds most loved by Allah are those done consistently, even if they are few (reported by al-Bukhari, no. 6464, and Muslim, no. 783 b). These words say exactly what counts when you learn: not one evening’s burst of enthusiasm, but what you are still doing six months later.

sections.title: Alone you start fast; together you go far
paragraphs: A proverb people often quote puts it simply: alone you go faster; together you go further. Someone who learns alone moves at their own pace, but they carry everything: the desire, the regularity, the correction. The day the enthusiasm fades, nothing holds them back.

In a group, everyone carries the others a little. You come because you are expected. You prepare because the others will have prepared. You hear a classmate recite a surah you thought was too long, and you tell yourself it can be done.

sections.title: What tradition says about Quran circles
paragraphs: Gathering around the Quran is a practice that tradition holds in particular honour. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said that no group of people gathers in one of the houses of Allah to recite the Book of Allah and study it together without tranquillity descending upon them, mercy covering them, the angels surrounding them, and Allah mentioning them to those who are with Him (reported by Muslim, no. 2699 a).

The Quran also invites us to choose our companions: in Surah Al-Kahf (Quran 18:28), it calls for patience in keeping company with those who call on their Lord morning and evening, seeking His Face. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) compared a good companion to a seller of musk and a bad one to a blacksmith (reported by al-Bukhari, no. 2101; see also al-Bukhari, no. 5534, and Muslim, no. 2628). And he warned that a person follows the religion of their close friend, so each of us should look at whom we take as a friend (reported by Abu Dawud, no. 4833, and at-Tirmidhi, no. 2378; a hadith graded hasan).

So a group is not just a convenient way to learn. It is part of how tradition understands knowledge: we learn with others, and we help one another, as the Quran invites us to in Surah Al-Ma’idah (Quran 5:2): to help one another in goodness and piety, and not in sin and transgression.

sections.title: An ambitious group, not just any group
paragraphs: Not every group carries you along. A group that meets without a goal, without a schedule and without a teacher often ends up drifting apart. What makes a class strong is a shared aim, a fixed appointment, and someone who guides and corrects.

Healthy emulation has its full place there. The Quran says it plainly: in Surah Al-Baqarah (Quran 2:148), it calls on us to race one another in good deeds. And, about the delights promised to believers, Surah Al-Mutaffifin (Quran 83:26) says that this is what those who strive should compete for. Competing in goodness is not comparing yourself to put yourself down; it is pulling one another upwards.
Size matters too. Too big, and a group lets everyone disappear; too small, and it depends on a single absence. A small class lets every student recite, be heard and be corrected at every session.

sections.title: How Rewayah Academy classes work
paragraphs: Rewayah Academy built its classes on this principle. Every student joins a stable class, with the same teacher and the same schedule every week. The class progresses together, step by step, and each step has a planned length and a deadline: the programme moves forward, it does not drag on endlessly.

For children and teenagers aged 6 to 17: three one-hour sessions a week, including a five-minute break, in a class of 3 to 5 students. For adults: three sessions of an hour and a half a week, including a ten-minute break, in a class of 3 to 6 students. A class opens as soon as three students are enrolled.

For a child, the parent can join the session as a silent observer when the class is open to observers: two visits of at most two minutes per session, so four minutes at most. At the end of each week, the parent receives the teacher’s weekly report. A beginner starts with the basics: the letters, reading with vowel marks, reading in the Quran, then the short surahs, from Al-Fatiha to Az-Zalzalah.
If this way does not suit you, others exist, run by other people.

A quality reviewer may attend sessions. Sensitive access is recorded in a log.

sections.title: Live sessions and recording
paragraphs: Video goes through a specialised service. Access to a session is granted by the server, for that session only and for a short time.
At present, the app does not record classes. If recording comes back, we will tell you beforehand why, how long it is kept and who can access it, and we will ask for your consent.
A notice in the classroom reminds everyone that a quality-check visit is possible.

sections.title: Where your information is
paragraphs: We use a web page host, a database with account sign-in, a video service, private file storage, a payment provider and an error-reporting service. They process your information on our behalf, for these reasons only.

To protect sign-in against bots, we use Cloudflare Turnstile (Cloudflare, Inc.). During the check, Cloudflare processes your IP address and technical information about your browser, only for this check and without any advertising cookie. Legal basis: our legitimate interest in securing the service.
The database is hosted in Ireland, in the European Union. Other providers may process some information outside the United Kingdom: these transfers follow the safeguards provided for by law.

sections.title: How long
paragraphs: We keep each type of information for as long as necessary, and no longer. A teacher’s identity document is deleted at the end of a set period. A deletion may be put on hold in the event of a dispute.

Account and profile: as long as the account exists. After a deletion request and a 14-day cooling-off period, the name, e-mail address and contact details are erased. Invoices and payments: 6 years, as required by UK accounting law. A teacher’s identity document: 90 days at most after verification. Messages: as long as the account exists; after deletion, their author becomes anonymous.

sections.title: Your rights
paragraphs: See the information we hold about you.
Correct it.
Ask for it to be deleted or limit its use.
Write to us. We first check that it is really you, or the student’s guardian. You can also contact the data protection authority in your country.

sections.title: Security
paragraphs: Access rules are enforced by the server. Identity documents are kept in a private space, separate from photos. No protection is absolute: if you see a problem, write to us.

sections.title: Children
paragraphs: A child’s information is provided and managed by their guardian. See the Child protection text.

/fr/legal/cookies.title: Cookies | Rewayah Academy
/fr/legal/cookies.description: What the Rewayah Academy app and website keep on your device.
/fr/legal/cookies.intro: Version 2026-10-v1, text of 18 October 2026. The app and the website keep very little on your device. Here is what.

sections.title: What it is
paragraphs: A cookie or local data is a small item kept by your browser or your device. It helps a service recognise you or remember a setting.

sections.title: What the app keeps
paragraphs: Your sign-in session.
Your display preferences, such as language and theme.
A limited cache, which you can clear.
On a student’s device, their personal code, which never leaves the device.
These items are necessary for the app to work.

sections.title: What we do not use
paragraphs: As of the date of this text, neither the app nor the website uses advertising cookies or audience measurement.

sections.title: Error reports
paragraphs: When the app crashes, a technical report may be sent to an error-tracking service. It contains no screenshot, no name and no identity.

sections.title: Controlling them
paragraphs: You can clear the website’s data in your browser settings, or sign out from Account. You will then need to sign in again and redo your display settings.

sections.title: Third-party services
paragraphs: If you leave Rewayah Academy for another service, for example for payment, that service applies its own rules.

/fr/accessibilite.title: Accessibility | Rewayah Academy
/fr/accessibilite.description: Status of the accessibility checks on the Rewayah Academy website, and how to report a difficulty.
/fr/accessibilite.h1: Accessibility of the Rewayah Academy website
/fr/accessibilite.intro: We want everyone to be able to read and use this website: with a keyboard, with zoom or with assistive technology.

sections.title: A website more people can use
paragraphs: The text can be read without animations or images. Headings follow in order, every link says where it leads, and the pages can be used with a keyboard.
If your device asks for reduced motion, the website stops its animations. On a small screen or with zoom, the text reflows.

sections.title: Status of the checks
paragraphs: This website has not yet been fully checked against the WCAG 2.2 level AA standard. If a page causes you trouble, write to support@rewayahacademy.com: we will fix it.

sections.title: Reporting a difficulty
paragraphs: Describe the page and the difficulty to support@rewayahacademy.com. Do not send any personal information about a child in your report.
